extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, practitioners before the USPTO, OED attorneys and adjudicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary guidance used in Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) proceedings to evaluate attorney misconduct (37 C.F.R. rules), pro hac vice/local court practice issues, neglect, and factors for imposing sanctions. Focused on conduct that affects practice before courts and the PTO and the penalties calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance from Poole: 'disreputable' conduct generally includes 'unprofessional' conduct and 'any conduct violative of the ordinary standard of professional obligation and honor.' Example application: noncompliance with court orders that results in dismissal of a client's case constitutes disreputable/gross misconduct. The tribunal defers to contemporaneous court findings about attorney misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically includes conduct that negatively impacts the public's perception or efficacy of the courts or legal profession. Examples: failure to adequately or properly represent a client; tardiness or absence from trial; failure to appear on behalf of a client; failure to communicate with a client; failure to prosecute a claim; failure to inform a client of suspension. Case citations (Schroeder, Attorney Grievance Comm’n v. Rand, Brown) are used to support scope. The tribunal assesses repeated/pattern behavior (e.g., repeatedly ignoring court orders) as prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) — neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall not neglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect does not require a showing of willfulness. Illustrative conduct: failing to timely respond or to respond at all to correspondence from the PTO or courts, failing to communicate with clients whose patent applications were abandoned for lack of cooperation, failing to take corrective action to revive applications. The tribunal treats failure to comply with court orders, correspondence, requests for information, and failure to take corrective action to prevent dismissal as neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(1) — failure to seek lawful objectives of a client
rubrics_metrics.description: "[a] practitioner shall not intentionally fail to seek the lawful objectives of a client through reasonably available means permitted by law and the Disciplinary Rules" (except as otherwise provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is grounded in the ABA Model Code (DR 7-101). Proof requires a showing of intentional failure; negligent or even grossly negligent conduct without clear and convincing evidence of intent is insufficient to establish a violation. Example: failure to prosecute a client's case can fall under this rule if shown to be intentional, but absent clear and convincing evidence of intent the tribunal will not find a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Rule LR 83.2(b) — Pro Hac Vice admission requirements (D.N.H. example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Local Rule describing pro hac vice admissions: an attorney may be permitted to practice in a particular action at the court's discretion and must remain associated with local counsel; the court may revoke permission for good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting affidavit must include: (A) office address and telephone; (B) listing of courts admitted to and dates; (C) statement of good standing and eligibility; (D) statement that attorney is not suspended or disbarred; (E) statement describing any disciplinary matters and prior felony/misdemeanor convictions; (F) disclosure/explanation of prior denials or revocations of pro hac vice status. Motion must be accompanied by published fee; associated local counsel must sign filings and attend proceedings unless excused. Failure to comply with such local rules can lead to dismissal or referral for appropriate action, but permissive language in an order ("may be referred") can affect determination of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for contempt and reliance on court findings
rubrics_metrics.description: District court stated: 'A party may be held in civil contempt for failure to comply with a court order if . . . the proof of noncompliance is clear and convincing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tribunal defers to contemporaneous district court findings made under the appropriate standard (e.g., clear and convincing) and regards those findings as more credible than years-later reconstructions. The standard for civil contempt is applied when evaluating underlying court contempt determinations relied upon in disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for independent authority/analysis for each charged rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director is instructed to 'provide authority and argument for why Respondent's conduct violated [each] specific rule independent of the other rules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors should avoid attempting to prosecute multiple rule violations based on the same underlying conduct without providing independent support and analysis for each rule alleged. Failure to do so may result in abandonment or dismissal of particular rule allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay of § 10.23(b)(6) (other conduct) with § 10.23(b)(1)-(5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of 'other conduct that adversely reflects on [an attorney's] fitness to practice' under § 10.23(b)(6) cannot stand if the conduct is already prohibited by § 10.23(b)(1)-(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If conduct falls within the scope of subsection (b)(1)-(5), it cannot separately be charged under (b)(6); tribunals have dismissed or treated as abandoned (b)(6) allegations when overlapping charges exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty factors for sanctions under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four factors must be considered before sanctioning a practitioner: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; (4) existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis of these factors is interrelated. The ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions provide guidance as to the existence and weight of aggravating and mitigating factors. Prior OED/PTO decisions (e.g., Schroeder, Burmeister, Chae) are cited for application of the factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions — aggravating/mitigating factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standards outline black-letter aggravating and mitigating factors to guide sanctions determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal uses the ABA Standards to identify aggravating factors (e.g., prior disciplinary offenses, pattern of misconduct, multiple offenses, refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing, vulnerability of victims, substantial experience in the practice) and mitigating factors (e.g., absence of prior discipline, personal or emotional problems, timely good faith effort to make restitution, full and free disclosure to disciplinary authority, inexperience in the practice). Specific factors should be assessed in context.
